2026 Federal Tax Brackets

The 2026 federal income tax brackets and standard deductions this site uses, for single and married-filing-jointly filers, with examples and paycheck use.

Gross pay estimates
A closer look

On this page

Standard deductionsSingle filer bracketsMarried filing jointly bracketsHow the brackets workHow this site uses these figuresWhat is not coveredCommon questions

Use your actual work schedule for a more useful estimate.

Standard deductions

Federal taxable income starts with gross pay minus the standard deduction for your filing status. These are the 2026 figures this site uses:

Filing statusStandard deduction
Single$16,100
Married filing jointly$32,200

Single filer brackets

Taxable income is gross pay minus the $16,100 standard deduction. The rate applies only to the income inside each band:

Taxable incomeRate
Up to $12,40010%
Over $12,400 to $50,40012%
Over $50,400 to $105,70022%
Over $105,700 to $201,77524%
Over $201,775 to $256,22532%
Over $256,225 to $640,60035%
Over $640,60037%

Married filing jointly brackets

Taxable income is gross pay minus the $32,200 standard deduction:

Taxable incomeRate
Up to $24,80010%
Over $24,800 to $100,80012%
Over $100,800 to $211,40022%
Over $211,400 to $403,55024%
Over $403,550 to $512,45032%
Over $512,450 to $768,70035%
Over $768,70037%

How the brackets work

Rates are marginal: earning $1 more into a higher band costs that band's rate on that $1 only — the lower bands keep their lower rates. Two worked examples, computed with the same figures the site's calculators use:

Single, $60,000 gross. Taxable income is $60,000 − $16,100 = $43,900. Federal tax is 10% × $12,400 = $1,240, plus 12% × $31,500 = $3,780, for $5,020 — an 8.4% effective rate on gross pay.

Married filing jointly, $100,000 gross. Taxable income is $100,000 − $32,200 = $67,800. Federal tax is 10% × $24,800 = $2,480, plus 12% × $43,000 = $5,160, for $7,640 — a 7.6% effective rate on gross pay.

These are federal income tax figures only. Payroll taxes are separate: Social Security takes 6.2% on wages up to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare takes 1.45% on all wages, and an additional 0.9% applies to wages over $200,000.

How this site uses these figures

The paycheck calculator and every take-home figure on this site follow the same order: subtract the standard deduction, apply the brackets above to the taxable income, then add FICA. State tax is computed separately by the state engine. Local taxes, exemptions, credits, and phaseouts are not modeled — the figures here and in the tools are estimates, not a tax return.

What is not covered

This site's calculators offer single and married filing jointly only, so head-of-household and married-filing-separately brackets are not listed here. These are 2026 figures; 2027 brackets will be added once the IRS publishes them.

Common questions

Are these the rates I pay on all my income?

No. Rates are marginal: each band's rate applies only to the income inside that band. Your effective rate — total tax divided by gross pay — is lower than your top (marginal) rate. On $60,000 as a single filer, the federal bill is $5,020, an 8.4% effective rate, even though the top band touched is 12%.

Does the standard deduction apply automatically?

The site's take-home figures subtract the standard deduction for your filing status before applying the brackets. If you itemize deductions instead, your taxable income — and your tax — will differ.

Do these brackets include Social Security and Medicare?

No. Federal income tax is separate from FICA. Social Security takes 6.2% on wages up to the $184,500 wage base, Medicare takes 1.45% on all wages, and an additional 0.9% applies to wages over $200,000.

General information, not tax advice. For your own return, check the IRS figures for your filing status and year, or consult a tax professional.
